# What AI Agents Are There? Will New AI Agents Replace the Lobster? | 2026 Overview | Think BIG

[Home](https://thinkbigtw.com/en/) / [Guides](https://thinkbigtw.com/guides/) / AI Agents

AI Agent Overview · 2026

# Will New AI Agents Replace the Lobster (OpenClaw)?

Think BIG Editorial

Grok, Claude, ChatGPT, Gemini and others are launching fast. This guide covers what AI Agents are available in 2026, how each charges for usage, what to do when quotas run out, and where OpenClaw fits for long-running tasks.

Last updated: 2026-10-02 | Data verified: 2026-09-30

New AI Agents will not make OpenClaw (the Lobster) obsolete — they are designed for different purposes. Each one is excellent. But for long-running tasks where cost control matters, brand AI Agents are not the first choice, though they are great for collaboration.

- Brand AI Agents tie costs to subscription quotas. They suit collaboration tasks within brand ecosystems (Gmail, Teams, WhatsApp).

- Open-source AI Agents (like OpenClaw, Hermes) let you choose your own model and pay per actual usage — suitable for 24/7 operations with predictable costs.

- The two types work well together: run OpenClaw for long-running routine tasks; use brand AI Agents for collaboration or ecosystem-specific work.

## Key Takeaway

Each one is excellent. But for long-running tasks where cost control matters, brand AI Agents are not the first choice — though they are great for collaboration.

## Common AI Agents in 2026

Data verified: 2026-09-30. Prices are from official brand websites. All prices shown in original currency; no self-calculated conversions. Labels: [Official] from brand website or blog; [Third-party] media only; [To verify] not disclosed by vendor.

### Two Main Types

- Brand AI Agents  — subscription-based, fixed monthly fee with usage quota. Examples: Claude, ChatGPT Agent, Gemini Spark, Grok Bot, Muse, Copilot Autopilot, Manus.

- Open-source AI Agents  — software is free; model usage fees paid directly to your chosen model provider, or use a local model for zero model fees. Examples: OpenClaw (Lobster), Hermes Agent.

### Claude (Anthropic)

- What it is : Anthropic's AI assistant, integrated background task completion (reports, research) since September 2026. [Official]

- How to use : Web, desktop app, mobile, Claude Code; all share one usage limit. [Official]

- Pricing : Free (limited); Pro and Max plans available — see [claude.com/pricing](https://claude.com/pricing). Usage limits reset on 5-hour and weekly cycles; paid plans can purchase usage credits. [Official]

- Available in Taiwan : Yes. [Official]

- Source : [claude.com/pricing](https://claude.com/pricing), verified 2026-09-30.

### ChatGPT Agent and dots (OpenAI)

- What it is : ChatGPT Agent uses a virtual browser to complete multi-step tasks; dots (launched 2026-09-29) is a 24/7 AI Agent with its own cloud computer, connected to 4,000+ apps. [Official]

- How to use : Select "agent" in ChatGPT tools or type /agent; dots is accessible via ChatGPT, Slack, and Teams. [Official]

- Pricing : Plus and Pro plans available — see [openai.com/chatgpt/pricing](https://openai.com/chatgpt/pricing/). ChatGPT Agent and Codex share the same agentic quota; dots is included in Pro and Business Premium. [Official]

- Available in Taiwan : ChatGPT Agent yes; dots availability [To verify]. [Official]

- Source : [ChatGPT agent help](https://help.openai.com/en/articles/11752874-chatgpt-agent), [dots launch](https://openai.com/index/introducing-dots/), verified 2026-09-30.

### Gemini Spark (Google)

- What it is : Google's 24/7 personal AI Agent that works in the background even when your device is off, connected to Gmail, Calendar, and Drive. [Official]

- How to use : Requires Google AI Pro or Ultra subscription; must be 18+ with a personal Google account. [Official]

- Pricing : AI Pro and AI Ultra plans available — see [gemini.google/subscriptions](https://gemini.google/subscriptions/). Usage calculated by computation, recovering every 5 hours up to a weekly cap. [Official]

- Available in Taiwan : Not on the exclusion list; actual availability [To verify].

- Source : [gemini.google/subscriptions](https://gemini.google/subscriptions/), verified 2026-09-30.

### Grok Bot (xAI)

- What it is : xAI's persistent AI teammate (launched August 2026) with its own cloud computer, browser and terminal; multiple can run simultaneously. [Official]

- How to use : Available on macOS, Windows, Linux, iOS, Android. [Official]

- Pricing : SuperGrok and SuperGrok Plus plans — both include Grok Bot. All Grok products share one weekly usage pool; heavy video or long tasks consume more quota. Extra Usage Credits available (web only, 1-year validity) — see [x.ai/pricing](https://x.ai/pricing). [Official]

- Available in Taiwan : No official country list published [To verify]. [Official]

- Source : [x.ai/pricing](https://x.ai/pricing), verified 2026-09-30.

### Muse (Meta)

- What it is : Meta's personal AI Agent (launched 2026-09-08) running in a dedicated virtual machine; can browse, fill forms, send emails, and make bookings. Confirms before sending or paying. [Official]

- How to use : iOS, Android app and muse.ai. Currently limited to the US; Canada opened 2026-09-18. [Official]

- Pricing : Free (limited); Power (5B Muse tokens/week) and Maximum (30B Muse tokens/week) plans available — see [meta.com/ai/muse](https://www.meta.com/ai/muse/). [Official]

- Available in Taiwan : Not currently available. [Official]

- Source : [Meta Newsroom](https://about.fb.com/news/2026/09/introducing-muse-personal-ai-agent/), verified 2026-09-30.

### OpenClaw — the Lobster (Open-source)

- What it is : OpenClaw is an open-source personal AI assistant, often called "the Lobster" in Taiwan. Installed on your own computer; accessed via WhatsApp, Telegram or other chat apps. Supports both local and cloud models. [Official]

- How to use : Runs on Windows and macOS. Can be used standalone or paired with Hermes for a dual-agent setup.

- Pricing : Software is free. Model costs depend on your chosen provider and actual usage. [Official]

- Available in Taiwan : Yes (self-install). [Official]

- Source : OpenClaw official documentation, verified 2026-09-30. → [Installation guide (中)](https://thinkbigtw.com/guides/openclaw-daizhuang/)

## Two Approaches: How They Differ

The following compares approach types only — no rankings, no scores.

Dimension
Brand AI Agents
Open-source AI Agents (e.g. OpenClaw, Hermes)
Pricing Fixed monthly fee with usage quota included Pay per actual usage to your chosen model provider; software is free

When quota runs out Wait for reset, upgrade, or purchase credits No quota concept; costs scale with usage; budget-driven control

24/7 operation Varies by plan; some continue when your device is off Requires your computer to stay on (local install); or use cloud model API remotely

Model flexibility Usually locked to the brand's own model Choose any model: subscription plan, API, or local model

Data location Subject to brand's privacy policy; typically in brand cloud Local install — data stays on your computer; messages still sent to model provider when using cloud models

Best for Brand ecosystem collaboration (Gmail, Teams, WhatsApp); short high-intensity tasks Long-running 24/7 routines; scheduled tasks; cost-controlled operations

Each one is excellent. But for long-running tasks where cost control matters, brand AI Agents are not the first choice — though they are great for collaboration.

## What To Do When Your Quota Runs Out

- Claude (Anthropic) : 5-hour segment limit plus weekly cap; paid plans can purchase usage credits. (Source: [official](https://support.claude.com/en/articles/11647753-how-do-usage-and-length-limits-work), verified 2026-09-30)

- ChatGPT Agent (OpenAI) : Monthly limit per plan; credits available for purchase. (Source: [official](https://help.openai.com/en/articles/12642688), verified 2026-09-30)

- Grok Bot (xAI) : Weekly pool resets; Extra Usage Credits available for purchase (web only). (Source: [official](https://docs.x.ai/grok/faq), verified 2026-09-30)

- Gemini Spark (Google) : Computation-based, recovers every 5 hours up to weekly cap; Pro/Ultra can purchase AI credits. (Source: [official](https://blog.google/products-and-platforms/products/google-one/google-ai-subscriptions/), verified 2026-09-30)

- Muse (Meta) : Upgrade or wait for free quota to recover. Power: 5B tokens/week; Maximum: 30B tokens/week. (Source: [official](https://www.meta.com/help/subscriptions/1021145227643680/), verified 2026-09-30)

General approach: route long-running background work to an open-source AI Agent (like OpenClaw, Hermes) — use brand AI Agents for collaboration tasks when needed. → [OpenClaw + coding agent collaboration](https://thinkbigtw.com/full-agent/)

## Frequently Asked Questions

Q: Will new AI Agents replace OpenClaw (the Lobster)?

The two serve different purposes and work well together. Common brand AI Agents in 2026 include Grok Bot (xAI), Claude (Anthropic), ChatGPT Agent and dots (OpenAI), Gemini Spark (Google), Muse (Meta), Copilot Autopilot (Microsoft), and Manus. Each one is excellent, but for long-running tasks where cost control matters, brand AI Agents are not the first choice — though they are great for collaboration. OpenClaw and Hermes, as open-source AI Agents, let you choose your own model, pay per actual usage, and run 24/7.

Q: What AI Agents are available in 2026?

Two main types: (1) Brand AI Agents — subscription-based with usage quotas, such as Claude, ChatGPT Agent, Gemini Spark, Grok Bot, Muse, Copilot Autopilot, Manus. (2) Open-source AI Agents — software is free, you pay per model usage, such as OpenClaw (Lobster) and Hermes Agent.

Q: What should I do when my AI subscription quota runs out?

Common options: wait for quota reset, upgrade your plan, purchase additional credits, or route long-running background work to an open-source AI Agent (like OpenClaw) that charges per actual usage.

Q: Can brand AI Agents and OpenClaw be used together?

Yes. A common setup: OpenClaw handles 24/7 routine tasks; brand AI Agents handle collaboration tasks or ecosystem-specific work. → [OpenClaw + coding agent](https://thinkbigtw.com/full-agent/) / [Dual AI Agent plan](https://thinkbigtw.com/dual-agent/)

Q: Does Think BIG's pricing include AI model fees?

No. Think BIG's service fee covers installation and setup only. Third-party AI model usage fees are calculated based on your actual usage and paid directly to the model provider. See [FAQ](https://thinkbigtw.com/faq/).

## Sources and Update History

All data in this page is from official brand websites as of 2026-09-30. Numbers without official sources are not included.

# Thinking about abandoning your AI Agent? Ask these three questions first | Think BIG NEWS

[← Think BIG NEWS](https://thinkbigtw.com/en/news/)

Field Notes on AI Deployment · Issue 001
THINKBIGTW.COM

# THINK BIG

NEWS

SEEN BY AI

Friday, October 3, 2026
◆
First-hand observations on AI deployment
◆
Issue 001

AI Agent Deployment

## Thinking about abandoning your AI Agent? Ask these three questions first — and stop getting locked in

Think BIG Editorial  |  October 3, 2026

Most AI Agent abandonment has nothing to do with the tool itself. It comes down to three things nobody confirmed at the start: can you switch models, who owns the data, and can you predict the monthly cost? Get these three right upfront, and so-called "abandonment waves" will have nothing to do with you.

(Note: "Lobster" and "Hermes" are informal names used in the Taiwanese tech community for a category of AI Agent tools that can run continuously and operate the computer on your behalf. This article addresses deployment methodology for that type of tool, staying focused on the phenomenon without targeting any specific company or product.)

## 1.  The Situation: What the conversation is really about

AI Agents — AI assistants that can take action and complete tasks on their own — have moved over the past year from early-adopter experiments into real workflows. Alongside that shift came a familiar pattern: install it, use it for two or three weeks, lose interest, leave it gathering digital dust. This "abandonment" isn't unique to Taiwan; the whole industry is grappling with it.

A few independently verifiable observations from published research: industry analysts project that by 2027, more than 40%  of AI Agent projects may be abandoned or cancelled by businesses — and the cause is rarely the technology itself. The most common culprits are unclear governance and unexamined ROI assumptions.

One survey of senior executives found that roughly 80%  of respondents were concerned about "over-reliance on a single AI vendor." Separate reporting notes that after months of accumulated configuration and context, switching AI Agent providers is far from a simple URL swap — and switching costs keep rising.

In short, abandonment usually comes down to two underlying problems: starting without a clear use case, then discovering the tool doesn't fit ; and getting so embedded in a setup that you can't leave even when you want to . Whether the tool itself is good barely enters into it.

## 2.  The Debate: Two legitimate perspectives

The optimistic view  is that the core value of a continuously running AI Agent is precisely that you don't need to supervise it — it lives in your messaging app and on your computer, sends proactive reminders, reports on schedule, and learns your habits. For solo operators and small businesses, that's the equivalent of a tireless assistant who never clocks out.

The skeptical view  centres on three concerns: lock-in risk (model, data, and configuration all tied to one vendor), cost unpredictability (pricing structures vary widely across the market — fixed fee, usage-based, or hybrid — and the difference matters over a year), and maintenance burden (getting it running and keeping it stable are two very different things).

These perspectives don't actually contradict each other. The optimists are talking about the value ; the skeptics are talking about how to deploy without stepping on a landmine . Whether you end up abandoning the tool almost always comes down to whether you addressed those three skeptic concerns before you started.

◆ First-Hand Notes

## 3. What we learned from actually doing this

"Running" doesn't mean "running well."  We deployed a local AI setup on one machine that looked fine — it answered questions — but every single response took one to four minutes, sometimes timing out entirely. After a long diagnostic detour, we found the model had been running entirely on the CPU. The GPU was doing nothing. Now we check GPU utilization before we change anything else.

One verifiable metric is all you need.  For Ollama-based setups, ollama ps  shows the PROCESSOR column (100% GPU, 100% CPU, or a split). The API also returns video RAM usage (size_vram ). If video RAM usage is zero, it's running entirely on CPU  — regardless of how normal things look. We screenshot this number before every delivery.

The reason is usually not "not enough hardware."  Three root causes we've encountered, none of which require buying new equipment: the GPU wasn't detected (some integrated or hybrid graphics cards need extra environment configuration); the install path contained non-ASCII characters that crashed the detection process; the context window was set too large, which exhausted shared system memory and caused repeated crashes across the whole machine. AI memory is not "bigger is always better."

Nobody can promise perfect security.  What we can do is check every layer: scan skills before installation, pin versions, audit again before going live, and keep keys in system config rather than in plain text. This isn't "we're safer than others" — it's "we've checked everything that can be checked."

## 4.  Our recommendation: Three questions to answer before you deploy

Can you switch the underlying model?  Is the tool tied to a single AI provider, or can you swap models freely? An architecture that lets you choose and switch means that when a better or cheaper model appears, you can move. That's the exit you want to have.

Who holds the data?  Does it run on your own hardware, or on someone else's cloud? Local deployment keeps your data under your control. Cloud is also fine — but you should know exactly where your data sits before you commit.

Can you predict the monthly cost?  Fixed fee, or does it scale with usage? A plan where you can estimate costs in advance and stay within budget serves long-term operations far better than one where the bill might surprise you.

One line to close with: abandonment is decided before deployment, not by the tool.  Make sure you can switch models, that your data stays in your control, and that costs are predictable — and an AI Agent stops being a one-time experiment and starts being a genuine long-term collaborator.

◆ Editorial · How Think BIG approaches this

## What this architecture actually delivers

The three questions above are precisely what we lock down at the start of every deployment. The architecture we use delivers three concrete outcomes:

1. No single-model lock-in; API costs stay predictable.  The underlying model is interchangeable — switch to a lower-cost model when saving budget, switch to a higher-capability model when the task demands it. The same assistant can cost dramatically different amounts from month to month, and you control it.

2. Your data stays on your hardware.  Local deployment keeps records and configuration on your machine, not someone else's cloud.

3. Pinned versions, layered security review.  No automatic updates; every skill goes through a security check before going live — stable, maintainable, and auditable.

This is why the so-called "abandonment wave" doesn't touch the people who deploy this way: model flexibility, data ownership, and cost predictability are built in from day one.

### FAQ · Frequently Asked Questions

Q: Is it normal to stop using an AI Agent after a few weeks?
Very common. Industry projections suggest more than 40% of projects may be abandoned by 2027. But in most cases it's not the tool — it's that deployment started without clarifying the problem to solve, or whether the setup could be changed, or what the cost would look like.
Q: How do I know if an AI Agent will lock me in?
Check three things: can you choose and swap the underlying AI model; is the data on your machine or someone else's cloud; is the cost fixed or usage-based. Flexibility on all three keeps lock-in risk low.
Q: Local or cloud — which suits me?
Depends on the use case. If data residency matters, you want continuous operation, or you need predictable costs, local deployment makes more sense. For instant access without managing maintenance, cloud is more convenient. Both can be combined.
Q: What should I watch out for with third-party skills or plugins?
They typically have direct access to your files and accounts. Verify the source, run a basic security check, pin the version, and turn off auto-updates. Nobody can promise perfect security — the goal is to check every layer you can.

    Gartner-related projections on AI Agent project abandonment (via media reporting):
    [joget.com](https://joget.com/ai-agent-adoption-in-2026-what-the-analysts-data-shows/)
     ·
    2026 enterprise AI landscape survey (vendor dependency concerns):
    [kai-waehner.de](https://www.kai-waehner.de/blog/2026/04/06/enterprise-agentic-ai-landscape-2026-trust-flexibility-and-vendor-lock-in/)
     ·
    AI Agent switching costs reporting:
    [itbrew.com](https://www.itbrew.com/stories/ai-agents-vendor-switching)

# Google 排得上去，為什麼 ChatGPT 還是不提你？SEO 和 GEO 差在哪｜Think BIG NEWS

[← Think BIG NEWS](https://thinkbigtw.com/library/news/)

產業實測手記 · 第 003 期
THINKBIGTW.COM

# THINK BIG

NEWS

被　AI　看見

2026 年 10 月 7 日　星期三
◆
AI 導入的第一手觀察
◆
第 003 期

SEO · GEO · AI 能見度

## Google 排得上去，為什麼 ChatGPT 還是不提你？——SEO 和 GEO 差在哪

Think BIG 自媒體部　報導　|　2026 / 10 / 07

SEO 讓你在 Google 被找到，GEO 讓你在 AI 回答裡被提到。地基相同，但 AI 挑段落、也看別人怎麼講你，排名好不代表 AI 會提你。

## 一、 現象：大家開始「問 AI」，不只「搜尋」

2025 年 10 月 8 日，Google 在台灣正式推出繁體中文版「AI 模式」。官方說明，它會用「查詢展開」（query fan-out）把一個問題拆成多個子題、送出大量查詢，再整理成一段附連結的回答。ChatGPT 也會在問題需要最新資訊時自動上網查，回答附上可點開的來源。

使用者的習慣跟著變了。過去是打關鍵字、看十條藍色連結、自己點進去比較；現在越來越多人直接問一句完整的話，等 AI 給一個整理好的答案。Microsoft 2025 年 10 月的官方文章把這個變化講得很直白：在 AI 搜尋裡，重點不只是「被找到」，而是「被選中」。

於是出現一個很常見的困惑：我的網站在 Google 排得不錯，為什麼問 ChatGPT，它就是不提我？

先把兩個詞講清楚：

SEO（搜尋最佳化） GEO（生成式 AI 最佳化）
目標 在 Google 搜尋結果被找到、被點進來 在 AI 的回答裡被提到、被引用、被描述正確

對象 Google、Bing 的搜尋結果頁 ChatGPT、Gemini、Google AI 模式、Perplexity、Copilot

單位 整個頁面排第幾名 頁面裡的某一段，能不能被拿去組答案

看什麼 收錄、排名、點擊 有沒有被提到、有沒有附你的網址、描述對不對

## 二、 各方評價：官方說「地基一樣」，研究說「結果不一樣」

Google 的立場：先把 SEO 做好。  Google Search Central 的官方文件寫得很清楚：要出現在 AI 摘要（AI Overviews）或 AI 模式，沒有額外的要求，也不需要特別的優化；前提是頁面必須已被 Google 收錄，而且符合「能在搜尋結果顯示摘要」的條件。同一份文件也說，不需要建立新的機器可讀檔案、AI 文字檔，也沒有必須額外加的結構化資料。換句話說，在 Google 自家的 AI 功能裡，SEO 就是門票。

但其他 AI 用的不是 Google 的資料。  ChatGPT 的搜尋功能靠 OpenAI 自己的爬蟲 OAI-SearchBot 建索引，官方文件說，封鎖這個爬蟲的網站「不會出現在 ChatGPT 的搜尋回答裡」。Perplexity 也有自己的 PerplexityBot。所以「Google 排得上去」只代表 Google 看得到你，其他 AI 要另外確認。

AI 挑的是「段落」，不是「頁面」。  Microsoft 的官方文章說明，Copilot 這類 AI 助理不會從頭到尾讀一頁，而是把內容拆成小段，逐段評估，再從多個來源組成答案。它給的建議很具體：標題、說明和 H1 要一致；用清楚的小標切開段落；答案寫成一兩句就能獨立成立；用條列和比較表；重要資訊不要藏在分頁標籤、圖片或 PDF 裡。文中也承認，沒有任何祕訣能確定被 AI 選中。

學術研究：有效果，但沒有穩定的公式。  普林斯頓大學等團隊在 KDD 2024 發表的〈GEO: Generative Engine Optimization〉，在他們建立的測試集裡發現，加上引述、統計數字、引用來源等改寫方式，最多能讓內容在 AI 回答中的能見度提升約 40%。不過，2026 年一篇回顧 45 篇研究的綜述結論比較保守：最能重現的因素是「內容跟問題有多相關」和「在上下文裡的位置」；目前沒有任何一種技巧，被證明能長期、跨平台、穩定地提升被發現的機會。

平台的紅線也越來越清楚。  Google 的垃圾內容政策已明文把「試圖操縱 Google 搜尋中生成式 AI 的回答」列為違規手法；大量產出低價值頁面也屬於「大規模濫用內容」。想靠隱藏文字、灌頁面騙 AI，是走錯方向。

◆ 第一手手記

## 三、我們自己的官網：Google 有起色，AI 還是很少提我們

2026 年 10 月初，我們用同一套標準替自己的官網做了一次六層體檢：技術地基、內容寫法、結構化資料、權威與身分、站外可被引用性、量測。

站內三層八到九成，站外兩層兩到三成。  技術地基、結構化資料、量測三層都拿到八到九成；但「權威與身分」和「站外可被引用性」兩層，只有兩到三成。差距不在官網本身，在官網以外。

Google 排得上去，AI 卻很少提到我們。  Google Search Console 顯示，我們幾篇指南頁已經排進相關關鍵字的搜尋結果第一頁。但我們用同樣主題、換成「問 AI」的問法跑了一輪查詢，幾乎看不到自己，連一篇標題就是那句問題原文的指南頁，那一輪也沒有被拿去當答案。（只跑一輪的結果統計上並不可靠，這是我們後來修正量測方法的起點，下一期專文說明。）

AI 對我們的描述，甚至會錯。  我們曾問某個 AI 聊天工具我們公司是做什麼的，它很肯定地說我們「跟 AI 無關」。這說明 AI 對一家小公司的印象，來自它碰得到的少數資料；資料不夠或不一致，它就自己拼湊。

我們已經做的事：  robots.txt 開放主要 AI 爬蟲、首頁第一段就是一句完整的公司定義句、每頁都有結構化資料、公司名稱與描述在各處統一、每篇 NEWS 同步出英文版。我們還在補的事：站外被提到——具名的媒體露出、公開名錄登錄、以公司名義發表的社群長文。

這次體檢讓我們學到最重要的一件事：SEO 做好了，只是讓 AI「找得到」你；要讓 AI「說出」你，還需要別人也在講你，而且講得一致。

## 四、 我們的建議：SEO 和 GEO 一起做，分開量

先確認 Google 和 AI 都進得來。  重要頁面要被 Google 收錄、能顯示摘要；robots.txt 不要誤擋 OAI-SearchBot、PerplexityBot 這類搜尋用爬蟲。（要不要開放「訓練用」爬蟲是另一個決定，可以分開設定。）

把每一段寫成能單獨被引用的樣子。  一個小標回答一個問題，第一兩句就給答案，數字、定義、步驟、比較表寫清楚。這對 Google 的摘要和 AI 的段落挑選都有幫助。

讓你的「身分」在網路上一致。  公司全名、簡稱、地址、電話、服務描述，在官網、Google 商家檔案、社群簡介、公開名錄都用同一套說法。

累積真實的站外提及。  公協會與政府公開名錄、Google 商家檔案、具名媒體投稿、自家具名的社群長文與影片。不要找人在論壇假裝網友推薦：以 Dcard 為例，官方公告把口碑操作、品牌推廣的業配帳號列為永久停權對象；以消費者口吻推薦卻沒揭露利益關係，也可能違反公平會的薦證廣告規範。

分開量，不要混在一起看。  Google 的表現看 Search Console；Copilot 和 Bing 的 AI 引用，可以看 Bing Webmaster Tools 2026 年 2 月推出的 AI Performance 報表（公開預覽中）；ChatGPT、Perplexity 等 AI 的回答，要用重複抽樣的方法量。

一句話收尾：SEO 讓 AI 找得到你，GEO 讓 AI 說得出你。  兩件事地基一樣，終點不一樣。

◆ 編按 · Think BIG 的做法

## 這套架構實際帶來什麼

我們把 Think BIG 官網當第一個實驗場，先把自己從頭做一遍，再把同一套方法提供給企業：Think BIG 搜尋能見度服務（SEO＋GEO）——被 Google 找到，也被 AI 說出來。

一次體檢，兩邊都看：  Google 這邊看收錄、技術地基、關鍵字現況和頁面寫法；AI 這邊看各個 AI 有沒有提到你、怎麼描述你、引用了哪些來源。最後合併成一份「先做哪三件」的清單。

同一篇內容，兩邊都顧：  寫內容時同時照 SEO（關鍵字、標題、內部連結）和 GEO（答案前置、可被摘錄、站外佈局）的要求寫，不做兩套。

量測講方法：  AI 的回答每次都可能不同，我們用重複抽樣、按 AI 分開報告，不拿一次截圖當結論。

只做合規的事：  不買連結、不刷點擊、不養假帳號、不寫假評論、不做隱藏文字。我們不承諾名次或業績，承諾把該做的做對，每個月給你看得到的數據。

### 常見問答 · FAQ

Q1：SEO 和 GEO 有什麼不同？
SEO 是讓你的網頁在 Google、Bing 的搜尋結果被找到；GEO 是讓 ChatGPT、Gemini、Perplexity 這類 AI 在回答問題時提到你、引用你的網頁，而且描述正確。兩者都需要網站能被收錄、內容清楚，但 AI 是挑段落組答案，也很看重其他網站怎麼講你。
Q2：我在 Google 排名很好，為什麼 ChatGPT 不提我？
ChatGPT 的搜尋用的是 OpenAI 自己的爬蟲和索引，不是直接沿用 Google 排名；而且很多問題它不上網查，直接靠模型記憶回答。加上 AI 挑的是能獨立成立的段落，以及多個來源一致的說法，所以 Google 排名好，不代表會被 ChatGPT 提到。
Q3：要出現在 Google 的 AI 摘要，需要額外做什麼嗎？
依 Google 官方文件，沒有額外要求，也不需要特別的檔案或結構化資料。頁面必須被 Google 收錄，並且符合在搜尋結果顯示摘要的條件。把 SEO 基本功做好，就是進入 Google AI 功能的前提。
Q4：做 GEO 需要 llms.txt 嗎？
Google 官方文件說明，出現在 AI 摘要和 AI 模式不需要建立新的機器可讀檔案或 AI 文字檔。可以放，但不要把它當成重點；可被收錄、段落清楚、身分一致、站外有真實提及，影響比較大。
Q5：怎麼知道 AI 有沒有提到我的公司？
不要只問一次就下結論，AI 的回答每次都可能不同。建議同一題換幾種問法、每題重複問多次、連續追蹤幾週，並分開記錄「有沒有提到你」「有沒有附你的網址」「描述對不對」。Copilot 和 Bing 的引用情況，也可以看 Bing Webmaster Tools 的 AI Performance 報表。

# You Rank on Google. So Why Doesn’t ChatGPT Mention You? SEO vs. GEO, Explained | Think BIG NEWS

[← Think BIG NEWS](https://thinkbigtw.com/en/news/)

Field Notes · Issue 003
THINKBIGTW.COM

# THINK BIG

NEWS

被　AI　看見

October 7, 2026 · Wednesday
◆
First-hand observations on AI deployment
◆
Issue 003

SEO · GEO · AI Visibility

## You Rank on Google. So Why Doesn’t ChatGPT Mention You? — SEO vs. GEO, Explained

Think BIG Editorial  |  October 7, 2026

SEO gets you found in search results. GEO gets you mentioned in AI answers. Same foundation, different finish line: AI picks passages and weighs what others say about you, so ranking well doesn’t mean AI will name you.

## 1.  What’s happening: people are asking AI, not just searching

On October 8, 2025, Google launched AI Mode in Traditional Chinese for users in Taiwan. AI Mode uses a “query fan-out” technique: it breaks a question into subtopics, runs many searches at once, and returns a synthesized answer with links. ChatGPT also searches the web automatically when a question would benefit from current information, and its answers include clickable citations.

User behavior is shifting. Instead of typing keywords, scanning ten blue links, and comparing pages themselves, more people now ask a full question and wait for an AI to hand back an answer. A Microsoft post from October 2025 put it plainly: in AI search, it’s not just about being found — it’s about being selected .

That leads to a question we hear constantly: “My site ranks well on Google. Why won’t ChatGPT mention us?”

SEO (Search Engine Optimization) GEO (Generative Engine Optimization)
Goal Get found and clicked in search results Get mentioned, cited, and described accurately in AI answers

Where Google and Bing results pages ChatGPT, Gemini, Google AI Mode, Perplexity, Copilot

Unit Where a whole page ranks Whether a specific passage gets pulled into an answer

Track Indexing, rankings, clicks Mentions, citations of your URL, accuracy of description

## 2.  What the sources say: official docs say “same foundation,” research says “different outcomes”

Google’s position: get your SEO right first.  Google Search Central states there are no additional requirements to appear in AI Overviews or AI Mode, and no special optimizations needed. A page must be indexed and snippet-eligible. The same page says you don’t need new machine-readable files, AI text files, or special schema.org markup. In other words, for Google’s own AI features, SEO is the ticket in.

Other AI tools don’t use Google’s index.  ChatGPT search relies on OpenAI’s own crawler, OAI-SearchBot. OpenAI’s documentation says sites that block it will not be shown in ChatGPT search answers. Perplexity runs its own crawler, PerplexityBot. Ranking on Google only tells you Google can see you. Everything else needs to be checked separately.

AI selects passages, not pages.  Microsoft explains that assistants like Copilot don’t read a page top to bottom. They break content into smaller pieces, evaluate each one, and assemble an answer from multiple sources. The practical advice: keep the title, description, and H1 aligned; use clear subheadings to separate ideas; write answers that stand on their own in one or two sentences; use lists and comparison tables; don’t bury key information in tabs, images, or PDFs. The same post acknowledges there’s no secret formula that ensures selection.

Research: real effects, no stable formula.  The paper that coined the term, “GEO: Generative Engine Optimization” (Princeton and collaborators, KDD 2024), found that rewrites such as adding quotations, statistics, and citations could boost visibility in AI responses by up to about 40% on the authors’ benchmark. A 2026 review of 45 studies is more cautious: topical relevance and position in context are the most reproducible levers, and no reviewed technique shows a stable, long-term, cross-platform causal effect.

Platform rules are getting sharper.  Google’s spam policies now explicitly list attempts to manipulate generative AI responses as a spam technique, and mass-producing low-value pages falls under scaled content abuse. Hidden text and page farms aimed at AI are a dead end.

◆ First-hand notes

## 3. Our own website: Google is warming up, AI still rarely mentions us

In early October 2026, we ran our own site through a six-layer audit: technical foundation, content, structured data, authority and entity, off-site citability, and measurement.

On-site layers scored 80–90%. Off-site layers scored 20–30%.  Technical foundation, structured data, and measurement all landed in the 80–90% range. “Authority and entity” and “off-site citability” landed at 20–30%. The gap wasn’t on our website. It was everywhere else.

Google ranks us; AI rarely brings us up.  Google Search Console shows several of our guides on the first page of results for their target queries. But when we ran a round of the same topics phrased as questions to AI, we barely showed up. Even a guide whose headline is that exact question wasn’t used as a source in that round. (A single round isn’t statistically reliable — that realization is what pushed us to rebuild our measurement method, which we cover in the next issue.)

AI has even described us incorrectly.  We once asked an AI chatbot what our company does, and it said, with full confidence, that we had nothing to do with AI. An AI’s picture of a small company comes from the little information it can reach. When that information is thin or inconsistent, it fills in the blanks.

What we’ve done:  opened robots.txt to major AI crawlers including OAI-SearchBot and PerplexityBot; put a complete one-sentence company definition at the top of our homepage; added Organization, Article, and FAQ structured data across the site; standardized our name and description everywhere; published an English edition of every NEWS article because research shows ChatGPT cites a large share of English sources when answering questions about Taiwan.

What we’re still building:  off-site mentions. Bylined media coverage, public directory listings, and long-form posts on our own named social accounts. We won’t fill the gap with fake accounts or paid forum posts.

The biggest lesson: good SEO makes you findable to AI. Getting AI to actually say your name takes other people talking about you, consistently.

## 4.  Our recommendations: do SEO and GEO together, measure them separately

Make sure both Google and AI crawlers can get in.  Key pages should be indexed and snippet-eligible. Check that robots.txt doesn’t accidentally block search crawlers like OAI-SearchBot or PerplexityBot. (Whether to allow AI training  crawlers is a separate decision.)

Write every section so it can be quoted on its own.  One subheading, one question. Put the answer in the first sentence or two. Spell out numbers, definitions, steps, and comparisons. This helps both Google snippets and AI passage selection.

Keep your identity consistent across the web.  Use the same legal name, short name, address, phone number, and service description on your website, Google Business Profile, social bios, and public directories.

Earn real off-site mentions.  Think industry association and government directories, Google Business Profile, bylined media contributions, and long-form posts on your own named accounts. Don’t hire people to pose as happy customers on forums. Dcard, a popular anonymous forum in Taiwan, permanently bans accounts used for word-of-mouth marketing, and an undisclosed paid endorsement in a consumer’s voice may violate Taiwan Fair Trade Commission rules on endorsement advertising.

Measure each channel on its own terms.  Use Search Console for Google; for Copilot and Bing, use the AI Performance report in Bing Webmaster Tools (public preview since February 2026); for ChatGPT, Perplexity, and other AI answers, use repeated sampling.

Bottom line: SEO lets AI find you. GEO gets AI to say your name.  Same foundation, different finish line.

◆ Editor’s note · How Think BIG approaches this

## One audit. Both sides. Built into every piece of content.

(The following reflects Think BIG’s own position and is separate from the neutral reporting above.)

We used our own website as the first test case, working through everything ourselves before offering the same method to businesses: Think BIG Search Visibility (SEO + GEO) — get found on Google, get named by AI.

One audit, both sides:  Google side covers indexing, technical foundation, keyword standing, and on-page writing. AI side covers whether each AI mentions you, how it describes you, and which sources it cites. Both roll up into one “top three things to fix first” list.

One piece of content, both jobs:  every piece is written for SEO (keywords, titles, internal links) and GEO (answer first, quotable passages, off-site placement) at the same time.

Measurement with a stated method:  AI answers change from run to run, so we use repeated sampling and report each AI separately. One screenshot is never a conclusion.

Compliant by design:  no bought links, no click farms, no fake accounts, no fake reviews, no hidden text. We don’t promise rankings or sales results. We promise to do the right things well and show you the numbers every month.

### FAQ

Q1: What’s the difference between SEO and GEO?
SEO helps your pages get found in Google and Bing search results. GEO helps AI tools like ChatGPT, Gemini, and Perplexity mention you, cite your pages, and describe you accurately when they answer questions. Both require indexable sites and clear content, but AI assembles answers from individual passages and gives weight to what other sites say about you.
Q2: I rank well on Google. Why doesn’t ChatGPT mention me?
ChatGPT search uses OpenAI’s own crawler and index rather than Google’s rankings, and for many questions it doesn’t search at all, answering from what the model already learned. It also favors passages that stand on their own and claims that multiple sources agree on. A strong Google ranking doesn’t carry over automatically.
Q3: Do I need to do anything extra to appear in Google’s AI Overviews?
According to Google’s documentation, no. There are no additional requirements, special files, or required structured data. The page must be indexed and eligible to show with a snippet in Google Search. Solid SEO fundamentals are the prerequisite.
Q4: Do I need an llms.txt file for GEO?
Google says you don’t need new machine-readable files or AI text files to appear in AI Overviews or AI Mode. You can add one, but don’t treat it as a priority. Indexability, clear passages, a consistent identity, and genuine off-site mentions matter more.
Q5: How can I tell whether AI mentions my company?
Don’t judge from a single question. AI answers vary from run to run. Ask the same question several ways, repeat each one multiple times, track it over several weeks, and record separately whether you were mentioned, whether your URL was cited, and whether the description was accurate. For Copilot and Bing, check the AI Performance report in Bing Webmaster Tools.

[Chat on LINE](https://lin.ee/n5KW430)

Two channels, one foundation

## Two ways customers find you — both need to work

Today's customers find you in two very different ways. Both rely on the same underlying foundation, so doing them separately is wasteful — doing them together is efficient.

### Channel 1: Google Search (SEO)

When a customer types your industry and location into Google, where do you rank?

- How many of your pages Google has indexed, which important pages are missing

- Mobile usability, page speed, and technical architecture issues

- Title tags, descriptions, and structured data correctness

- Local search and Google Business Profile completeness

- Where you currently rank for the keywords your customers actually search

### Channel 2: AI Answers (GEO)

A growing share of customers ask ChatGPT, Perplexity, or Google AI directly: "Which company in this category is recommended?"

- Whether 5 major AI platforms mention you, and how they describe you

- Which sources the AI cites, and how competitors compare

- Whether the AI has described you incorrectly (wrong address, missing services, confusion with another brand)

- Whether the AI answered from training memory or actually retrieved your site

- Different AI platforms prefer entirely different sources — what works for one may not work for another

Both channels rely on the same foundation: a crawlable site, well-structured content, a consistent identity across platforms, and credible off-site mentions. We address all of this together — no duplicated work, no conflicting advice.

SEO vs GEO

Service phases

## Audit → Foundation Build → Monthly Management

The audit comes first. The foundation build is next. Monthly management is ongoing — not a subscription you can skip to.

SEO + GEO Visibility Audit

One-time · Prerequisite

Google Search Audit deliverables (SEO):

- Index coverage:  how many pages Google has indexed, which important pages are missing (via site: query and Search Console if authorized)

- Technical foundation:  mobile usability, HTTPS, Core Web Vitals public data, sitemap/robots, duplicate URLs and canonicals, broken links

AI Visibility Baseline deliverables (GEO):

- Competitor mention comparison:  who the AI mentioned for the same questions, and how often (factual record only)

- Retrieval trigger log:  for each question, whether the AI answered from training memory or actually retrieved your site (two different gaps, two different fixes)

- Error and confusion inventory:  what the AI has gotten wrong about you — outdated address, missing services, confusion with a same-name company — each item sourced and ranked by priority

- Per-AI action list:  different AI platforms prefer entirely different source types, so your action list is broken down by platform, not given as a single universal prescription

- Methodology page:  which questions, which day, which AI version, how many repetitions — you can re-run the same queries and verify our numbers

- Compliant tactics only:  the report flags which approaches carry platform rule violations or legal risk in Taiwan, so you know what to avoid

For businesses without a website: we audit your Google Business Profile, marketplace listings, and social channels instead; the AI check works identically.

The report's final page combines SEO and GEO findings into a single prioritized "do these three things first" list. A debrief call is included after delivery.

- Internal linking clean-up

- Sitemap submission and Search Console setup assistance

- Content restructuring: answer-first writing, FAQ optimization, quotable fact statements

- Schema structured data implementation

- Entity consolidation: consistent name, sameAs links, directory registration

- First two off-site citable content pieces (government or trade directories, Google Business, Threads/YouTube long-form, named media submissions, review site listings — compliant channels only)

- Off-site roadmap document: per-AI-platform expansion directions for future months

For businesses without a website: the foundation build skips website changes and instead creates off-site content assets that AI platforms can cite.

Ongoing work and reporting after the foundation is in place. Each month's deliverables include a combination of content production, off-site placement, and a monitoring report.

- Content written for AI citation:  answer-first, clearly stated facts, Q&A and list formats — structured so it works for both SEO (keyword relevance, headings, internal links) and GEO (quotable, answer-first) at the same time

- Off-site placement:  government and trade directories, Google Business Profile, named Threads/YouTube long-form content, named media submissions, review site listings — distributed across multiple channels, not concentrated in one

- Identity alignment:  company name, social links, and directory information kept consistent across all platforms

Monthly report includes:

- Google Search section:  keyword rank tracking, Search Console impressions and click trends (with client authorization), technical anomaly alerts

- AI Visibility section:  mention rate trend (repeated sampling over multiple days, with confidence intervals), competitor mention comparison, source gap recommendations

- Our own site as a live demonstration:  we run the same process on thinkbigtw.com from scratch and report our own relative changes each month — so what you see is someone actually doing the work, not just a slide deck

We do not commit to specific rankings or citation counts. What we commit to is: real repeated-sampling data with confidence intervals that hold up statistically — not a single query screenshot.

Methodology

## Why we measure this way

The measurement method determines whether a report is worth trusting. We publish the methodology because transparency is the core of this service.

### Repeated sampling, not a single query

Academic research (University of St. Gallen, 2026) has confirmed that re-running the same question on the same day yields citations with only a 32–43% overlap. AI citation is a probability distribution — a single query is statistically near-meaningless. We query each question across multiple days, then review results manually to derive a defensible range.

### Per-AI breakdown, not a universal list

Taiwan field data shows: Gemini tends to cite official websites and review directories; Perplexity favors Threads and YouTube discussions; ChatGPT favors government institution directories and cites non-Chinese sources 70% of the time. Cross-platform source overlap is only 5–20%. Your action list is broken down by AI platform.

### Confidence intervals, not single-point numbers

For a brand detection rate to have a standard error below 0.10, you need at least 7 repetitions on the same day and a rolling window of 10+ days. Our reports only make claims supported by statistical evidence: if confidence intervals overlap, we write "no meaningful change," not a fabricated improvement figure.

### Retrieval trigger rate: memory vs. live retrieval

57% of ChatGPT responses to queries don't trigger a web search at all — the model answers from training memory, meaning your website is invisible to it regardless of how good it is. We log the trigger status per question; the two gap types require entirely different fixes.

### Methodology you can verify yourself

Every report includes: which questions were asked, on which dates, with which AI version, how many repetitions, API or browser, and region settings. You can take the same questions and re-run them yourself to verify our numbers aren't fabricated.

### SEO measurement: index, technical, keywords, local

- Index: site: queries and Search Console index status

- Technical: Core Web Vitals public data, mobile, HTTPS, canonicals

- Keywords: Search Console or manual queries, factual current-state report only

- Local: Google Business Profile completeness, map ranking position

Google official references: [SEO Starter Guide](https://developers.google.com/search/docs/fundamentals/seo-starter-guide), [AI Features and Your Website](https://developers.google.com/search/docs/appearance/ai-features)

What we never do

## Our hard limits — stated plainly

These practices are available in the market. We don't use them — not because we can't, but because they harm you.

✕

### Buying clicks or traffic

Artificially inflating clicks or purchasing traffic violates [Google's spam policies](https://developers.google.com/search/docs/essentials/spam-policies) and can result in your site being penalized or removed. We don't do it and don't recommend it.

✕

### Buying links or building PBNs

Link buying and private blog networks are explicitly cited violations in Google's spam policies. They may produce short-term effects but carry serious long-term risk. We only build genuine, sustainable off-site presence.

✕

### Posting commercial content on forums that prohibit it

Forums like Dcard and PTT explicitly prohibit commercial promotion in their rules. Getting caught means deleted posts, account bans, and reputational damage. We only produce named, compliant off-site content.

✕

### Fake reviews, sock-puppet accounts, anonymous astroturfing

Taiwan's Fair Trade Act prohibits content written in a third-party voice to mislead consumers. Any paid recommendation we produce is disclosed. We don't write fake reviews or maintain fake accounts.

✕

### Manipulating AI answers (hidden text, prompt injection)

Google explicitly listed "manipulating AI-generated answers" in its [spam policies](https://developers.google.com/search/docs/essentials/spam-policies) in 2026. Hidden text and prompt injection can get your site penalized or removed. Our approach is to make content genuinely worth citing — not to deceive the system.

✕

### Promising specific rankings or citation counts

Rankings are decided by Google. AI citations are probability distributions. Anyone who tells you "you will be on page one" or "AI will definitely recommend you" is telling you what you want to hear. We give you real data, not empty promises.

Honest timeline

## How long does it take? The honest version.

SEO and GEO both accumulate over time — they are not on/off switches. The following reflects typical patterns; actual timelines vary by industry competitiveness, how much verifiable information you make available, and AI platform algorithm changes.

Weeks 4–8

After content and page structure adjustments, initial movement starts appearing in both Google search and AI visibility.

Months 5–6

AI platforms start citing you in answers; Google keyword rankings show meaningful movement.

Months 6–12

Search and AI presence becomes more established; citation count shows a clear upward trend.

Factors that influence speed: how competitive your industry is, how much quantifiable information you are willing to publish, whether you have an existing website to improve, and AI platform algorithm changes (an external variable we monitor continuously).
We do not promise specific rankings or dates  — but you will see real monthly data showing how your search and AI visibility is developing.

FAQ

## Frequently asked questions

What is the difference between SEO and GEO, and why do them together?

SEO is about being found when someone searches on Google. GEO is about being cited when someone asks ChatGPT, Perplexity, or a similar AI a question. Both rely on the same foundation: a crawlable site, well-structured content, consistent identity across platforms, and credible off-site mentions. Doing them separately means duplicated effort — we audit and prioritize both together in one pass.

I don't have a website. Can I still use this service?

Yes. For businesses without a website, we audit your Google Business Profile, marketplace listings, directories, and social channels instead. The AI visibility check works identically. For the foundation build, we create off-site content assets rather than modifying a website.

Can you get me to the first page of Google?

Rankings are determined by Google — no one can promise you a specific position. We do not buy clicks, traffic, or links; those violate [Google's spam policies](https://developers.google.com/search/docs/essentials/spam-policies). What we commit to is doing the right work and providing verifiable monthly data so you can see your search and AI visibility develop over time.

How long before I see results?

SEO and GEO both accumulate — they are not on/off switches. In general: initial changes from content restructuring appear within 4–8 weeks; AI citations start to appear around months 5–6; noticeable presence growth comes around months 6–12. Actual timelines depend on industry competitiveness, how much verifiable information you publish, and AI platform algorithm changes. We do not commit to specific rankings or dates.

How do you measure AI visibility? Is it just a screenshot of one query?

No. We query five major AI platforms with 15–20 questions your customers would actually ask, repeated across multiple days. Academic research (University of St. Gallen, 2026) shows citation overlap between runs on the same question on the same day is only 32–43% — a single query is statistically near-meaningless. Our reports show a range with a confidence interval. Every report includes the full methodology — which questions, which day, which AI version, how many repetitions — so you can re-run the queries yourself and verify.

What do you never do?

We never buy clicks, traffic, or links; never create fake reviews or sock-puppet accounts; never post commercial content on forums that prohibit it; and never use hidden text or prompt injection to influence AI answers. Google explicitly listed AI answer manipulation in its spam policies in 2026. We build genuinely citable content — not gaming the system.

What do I need to provide to get started?

Three things: your industry, your brand name or URL (if you don't have a website, tell us where you sell), and the 3–5 competitors you care most about. We'll draft 15–20 questions your customers would actually ask an AI, share them with you first, then run the full check. For the Google search audit, Search Console read access makes the report significantly more complete — but it works without it too.

Is my information kept confidential?

Your brand information, competitor list, and any Search Console data you authorize us to read are used solely to produce your report. They are not used for other client research, not shared externally, and not used as marketing material. Client identities and cases are always kept confidential — we never name clients publicly. That is a baseline commitment.

## Ready to be found on Google
and cited by AI?

Start with an audit. Know exactly where you stand — then decide the next step.

# Is Your Local AI Actually Using the GPU? "Installed" Doesn't Mean "Running Well" | Think BIG NEWS

[← Think BIG NEWS](https://thinkbigtw.com/en/news/)

Field Notes on AI Deployment · Issue 002
THINKBIGTW.COM

# THINK BIG

NEWS

SEEN BY AI

Monday, October 5, 2026
◆
First-hand observations on AI deployment
◆
Issue 002

Local AI Deployment

## Is your local AI actually using the GPU? "Installed" doesn't mean "running well"

Think BIG Editorial  |  October 5, 2026

When a local AI model is painfully slow — minutes per response, or constant timeouts — the most likely cause isn't underpowered hardware. It's that the model is running entirely on the CPU, and the GPU is sitting idle. One command, ten seconds, and you'll know for certain.

(Note: This article uses Ollama as the illustrative example because it is one of the most common tools for running local models on a personal computer. The underlying principles apply to other runtimes; the specific commands differ.)

## 1.  The Situation: A well-documented gap

Running an AI model on your own machine — no subscription, no data leaving the building, available offline — has gone from an enthusiast experiment to a realistic option for individuals and small teams. The most common complaint that followed is a single sentence: "I installed it, but it's too slow to use."

The open-source community has documented this thoroughly. Ollama's GitHub issue tracker includes reports of models that "occasionally fall back to CPU, causing 100% CPU utilization, until a restart." ([ollama/ollama #13765](https://github.com/ollama/ollama/issues/13765)) Another thread describes a version update that caused models to stop using the GPU entirely. ([ollama/ollama #13320](https://github.com/ollama/ollama/issues/13320)) Published troubleshooting guides note that this failure mode is particularly insidious because it produces no error message  — an outdated driver, a disabled environment variable, and the model quietly falls back to CPU, while everything on screen looks normal. ([cmaven.github.io](https://cmaven.github.io/en/etc/ollama-multi-gpu-troubleshooting/), [localaimaster.com](https://localaimaster.com/blog/ollama-not-using-gpu))

In other words: a "slow local AI" is usually not a performance problem. It's a configuration problem that hasn't been noticed yet.

## 2.  The Debate: Is local deployment worth it?

The case for local deployment  is concrete: data stays on your hardware, there's no per-token bill anxiety, and the model can run around the clock as part of an AI Agent workflow. For anyone who cares about privacy or wants continuous AI presence without ongoing cloud costs, this is something cloud services simply can't offer.

The reservations  cluster around two points:

The setup threshold is higher than expected.  Driver version, environment variables, model size relative to video RAM, memory allocation — any one of these being wrong degrades the result significantly, and there's no obvious starting point for diagnosis.

Hardware has to match the model.  If the model is larger than the available video RAM, the overflow gets offloaded to the CPU. The official Ollama FAQ notes that models can end up in a "partial CPU, partial GPU" state. ([docs.ollama.com/faq](https://docs.ollama.com/faq)) That split slows everything down.

Both sides are pointing at the same thing: local AI can be excellent, but only after someone confirms it's actually running on the right hardware.

◆ First-Hand Notes

## 3. What we learned from actually doing this

"Looks fine" is the most dangerous state.  We had a machine where the model was installed, conversations worked, and nothing reported an error — but every response took one to four minutes, with occasional timeouts. We spent considerable time adjusting other settings before finally checking: the model had been running 100% on the CPU. The GPU was untouched. We now check GPU utilization before touching anything else.

One metric is all you need.  ollama ps  shows the PROCESSOR column — 100% GPU, 100% CPU, or a split. The API also returns video RAM usage (size_vram ). If size_vram  is zero, the model is on CPU,  regardless of what everything else looks like. We screenshot this number before every delivery.

Three root causes we've actually encountered  — none requiring a hardware upgrade:

The GPU wasn't detected.  Some newer integrated or hybrid graphics architectures aren't automatically recognized. They require additional environment configuration, and that configuration must be set for the specific user account that runs the model, not just the admin account.

The install path contained non-ASCII characters.  The detection process crashed silently when the path included characters outside standard ASCII. Moving to a plain ASCII path fixed it immediately — the kind of trap that never appears in any spec sheet.

The context window was set too large.  Setting the AI's memory (context window) too high exhausted shared system RAM and caused cascading system instability. Ollama defaults to 4096 tokens (per the official FAQ) — that's a reasonable baseline. Increasing it is fine, but it should be sized to the machine.

The difference after fixing it.  Same machine, same model — switching from CPU-only to actual GPU use took response time from "minutes per question" to "output starts within seconds." That's a configuration fix, not a hardware upgrade.

## 4.  Our recommendation: Three steps when local AI is slow

Check the PROCESSOR column first — before anything else.  Run ollama ps . 100% CPU means the GPU isn't being used; a CPU/GPU split usually means the model is larger than available video RAM. This takes ten seconds and can save hours.

Match model size to video RAM.  Bigger isn't always better. A smaller model that fits entirely in video RAM will often outperform a larger model that spills onto the CPU. Choose based on what your hardware can actually hold.

Make "confirm the GPU" a standing check.  Driver updates, software updates, and account changes can all silently revert to CPU. Check after any meaningful change — don't wait for "why is this slow again?" to surface the issue.

One line to close with: when local AI is slow, suspect the configuration before the hardware.  In most cases, the machine is capable enough — it just hasn't been used correctly yet.

◆ Editorial · How Think BIG approaches this

## What "delivered and running well" actually means

When we deploy a local AI Agent on a client's machine, "GPU actually running" is a mandatory pre-delivery check — not something we do only when a problem surfaces. Our delivery standard includes:

Evidence before handoff, not a verbal "it's installed."  We confirm which hardware the model is using and record the video RAM consumption. We also run a task that calls a tool — not just a chat response — and verify the response time. Screenshots are kept as delivery documentation.

Your data stays on your hardware.  Local deployment keeps records and configuration on your machine. The model can be swapped as better or lower-cost options emerge.

Pinned versions; no automatic updates.  A version update is one of the most common causes of GPU fallback. We pin the version and validate any update before applying it — stability over chasing the latest release.

The value of local AI only materializes once it's confirmed to be running on the right hardware. That confirmation is what we deliver before handing over the keys.

### FAQ · Frequently Asked Questions

Q: How do I check whether my local AI model is using the GPU?
For Ollama, run ollama ps  and look at the PROCESSOR column. 100% GPU means fully on GPU; 100% CPU means the GPU is not being used; a split ratio means only part of the model fits in video RAM.
Q: I have a dedicated GPU — why is the AI still running on CPU?
Common causes: outdated driver, an environment variable that has disabled GPU access, a model larger than available video RAM, or the GPU not detected by the software. Most of these produce no error message, so you have to check actively.
Q: My local AI takes minutes per response. Is my hardware too weak?
Not necessarily. In most cases we've investigated, the model was running entirely on CPU. Confirm GPU is being used before deciding to upgrade.
Q: Is a bigger model always better?
No. A model that doesn't fit in video RAM has part offloaded to CPU, which can make it slower than a smaller model that fits entirely on the GPU. Match model size to available video RAM.
Q: How large should I set the context window?
Ollama defaults to 4096 tokens. Increasing is fine, but each step up consumes more RAM; setting it too high can destabilize the whole machine. Increase gradually based on your hardware, not all at once.

Sources
    Ollama official FAQ (PROCESSOR column interpretation, default context 4096):
    [docs.ollama.com](https://docs.ollama.com/faq)
     ·
    Ollama GitHub #13765 (intermittent CPU fallback):
    [github.com/ollama/ollama/issues/13765](https://github.com/ollama/ollama/issues/13765)
     ·
    Ollama GitHub #13320 (update breaks GPU use):
    [github.com/ollama/ollama/issues/13320](https://github.com/ollama/ollama/issues/13320)
     ·
    Multi-GPU troubleshooting guide (driver version, silent CPU fallback):
    [cmaven.github.io](https://cmaven.github.io/en/etc/ollama-multi-gpu-troubleshooting/)
     ·
    Ollama GPU not used — common causes:
    [localaimaster.com](https://localaimaster.com/blog/ollama-not-using-gpu)

All named sources are linked inline; commands and default values are based on the official Ollama documentation current at time of publication.

# 問 AI 一次就下結論？AI 的回答是機率，不是名次——GEO 該怎麼量才算數｜Think BIG NEWS

[← Think BIG NEWS](https://thinkbigtw.com/library/news/)

產業實測手記 · 第 004 期
THINKBIGTW.COM

# THINK BIG

NEWS

被　AI　看見

2026 年 10 月 9 日　星期五
◆
AI 導入的第一手觀察
◆
第 004 期

GEO 量測 · AI 能見度

## 問 AI 一次就下結論？——AI 的回答是機率，不是名次，GEO 該怎麼量才算數

Think BIG 自媒體部　報導　|　2026 / 10 / 09

AI 每次回答都可能不同，同一題幾分鐘內重問，引用來源只重疊三到四成。想知道 AI 會不會提你，要同題重問多次、追蹤數週，看區間不看單次。

## 一、 現象：一張截圖，說不了什麼

「我問了 ChatGPT，它推薦我們耶！」「我問了三個 AI，都沒提到我們。」這兩種說法我們都常聽到，背後是同一個習慣：問一次，就當成結果。  這在傳統搜尋還說得過去，同一個關鍵字幾分鐘內重搜，排名通常差不多。但 AI 的回答不是這樣運作的。

瑞士聖加侖大學（University of St. Gallen）的研究團隊在 2026 年 4 月發表論文〈Don't Measure Once〉，專門研究這件事。他們在 2026 年 1 月到 3 月之間，每天用同一批問題問四個 AI 搜尋服務（ChatGPT、Perplexity、Google AI 模式、Gemini），涵蓋四個產業、每個產業 8 題，連續追蹤 45 到 46 天；另外還在同一天內對同一題重問最多 10 次。（來源：[arXiv 2604.07585](https://arxiv.org/abs/2604.07585)）

結果：

天天在換。  前一天和後一天比，被引用的來源平均只重疊 34% 到 42%。幾分鐘內重問，一樣在換。  同一題同一天重問，引用來源的重疊度平均只有 32% 到 43%，跟隔天比差不多。研究者的結論是：不穩定主要來自模型生成答案本身的隨機性，不是外在的演算法調整。

品牌比來源穩一點。  以「回答中提到哪些品牌」來看，隔天的重疊度是 45% 到 59%，比引用來源穩定。有些題目很穩、有些幾乎全換。  只看一兩題，看到的是那幾題的個性，不是整體能見度。

AI 不一定會上網查。  ChatGPT 有 57.8% 的回答完全沒有附引用，因為它只在特定問題才啟動網路搜尋，其他時候靠模型本身的記憶回答。

研究摘要裡有一句話很適合當這篇的標題：AI 搜尋的能見度，應該被描述成一個分布 ，而不是一個單點結果 。

## 二、 各方評價：要量多少次才夠？

研究給了具體的門檻。  同一篇論文用統計方法推算，要讓「某品牌被提到的比例」估得夠穩（標準誤低於 0.10），同一題每天至少要問 7 次 ；如果要看引用來源，至少 8 次。時間上，以單一品牌來看，連續追蹤 10 天 標準誤才會低於 0.10，追蹤 24 天可以再降到 0.05 以下；作者建議用兩到四週的滾動區間 來看數字。他們也建議：每個 AI 各自設基準線，不要把不同 AI 混成一個分數；監測時把「品牌有沒有被提到」當主要指標，「引用了哪些網址」當診斷用。

「多問幾次」也是偵測 AI 亂講的方法。 《Nature》2024 年刊登的研究提出：讓模型對同一題回答好幾次，如果答案的意思彼此對不上，就是它可能在亂編的訊號。（來源：[Farquhar 等，Nature 2024](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41586-024-07421-0)）一次的答案只是抽樣，重複才看得到真實樣貌。

技巧的效果，也要靠嚴謹量測才看得出來。  2026 年一篇回顧 45 篇 GEO 研究的綜述指出，商業稽核裡普遍出現「來源重疊低、每次結果差很多」的現象；而且目前沒有任何技巧被證明能長期、跨平台、穩定地提升被發現的機會。（來源：[arXiv 2607.14035](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.14035)）如果量測本身不穩，你根本分不出「是做法有效」還是「剛好抽到好結果」。

但不能為了量測去違規。  Google 的垃圾內容政策明文禁止「機器產生的流量」，也就是未經許可、用程式自動查詢 Google 搜尋，包括為了查排名去抓取結果。（來源：[Google 搜尋垃圾內容政策](https://developers.google.com/search/docs/essentials/spam-policies)）量測要走各 AI 的官方 API，再搭配人工抽查，並在報告裡說清楚用的是哪個通道。

官方數據也開始出現。  Bing Webmaster Tools 在 2026 年 2 月推出 AI Performance 報表（公開預覽），可以看到內容在 Copilot 與 Bing 的 AI 摘要中被引用的次數與頁面，以及隨時間的變化。（來源：[Bing 網站管理員部落格](https://blogs.bing.com/webmaster/February-2026/Introducing-AI-Performance-in-Bing-Webmaster-Tools-Public-Preview)）

◆ 第一手手記

## 三、我們自己量的時候，踩過的三個坑

我們做 AI 能見度服務之前，先拿我們的官網量。過程中踩了三個坑，後來都寫進了我們的量測方法裡。

坑一：只跑一輪，就以為看到真相。  我們第一次做基準線，是每題問一次、跑一輪。結果幾乎看不到自己，一度很挫折。後來對照 Google Search Console，才發現我們有幾篇指南在 Google 已經排進第一頁，跟那一輪的印象差很多。讀到聖加侖的研究後我們才確定：一輪的結果，統計上本來就撐不起任何結論。

坑二：測試環境不乾淨，答案會被污染。  2026 年 10 月 4 日，我們在內部用一個 AI 工具做代理測試，結果發現它讀到了測試電腦上我們自己的筆記，回答時把這些內容帶了進去。答案看起來很「懂我們」，但那不是一般使用者會看到的版本。OpenAI 的官方說明提到，開啟記憶功能時，ChatGPT 可能會用你存過的記憶來改寫搜尋查詢。從此我們規定：量測一律在乾淨的環境跑，不登入個人帳號、不帶對話紀錄、不帶記憶。

坑三：把「有提到」「有引用」「講對了」混成一件事。  AI 提到你的名字，不一定附你的網址；附了你的網址，描述也不一定正確。我們自己就遇過 AI 很肯定地把我們的營業項目講錯。所以現在每一次回答，我們都分開記錄：AI 有沒有上網查、有沒有提到我們、有沒有引用我們的網址、描述對不對。

踩完這三個坑，我們的量測方法改成這樣：

項目 我們現在的做法
題目 依意圖分層：泛問、情境、條件、品牌比較、事實型；每個意圖寫 3 到 5 種問法，含英文

鎖題 題庫建好就凍結，只加不改，數字才能前後比較

次數 每題每天每個 AI 重問多次，兩次之間至少隔 10 分鐘

天數 連續多天，用兩到四週的滾動區間看

分開看 每個 AI 各自一份基準線，不做跨 AI 平均

記錄 是否上網查、是否提到、提到的位置、是否引用網址、描述是否正確

呈現 每個數字附 95% 信賴區間；這期和上期的區間重疊，就寫「持平」，不說成長

通道 標明用的是 API 還是使用者介面；不自動化刷 Google 的頁面

## 四、 我們的建議：自己檢查的六個原則

如果你想自己看看 AI 有沒有提到你的公司：

1. 同一題換幾種問法。  客人怎麼問，你就怎麼問：「台中有哪些○○推薦？」「五個人的公司適合哪種○○？」「A 跟 B 差在哪？」

2. 每一題至少問 5 到 7 次。  記下這幾次裡有幾次提到你，用「幾成」來看，不要用「有或沒有」來看。

3. 用乾淨的環境。  登出帳號或用無痕視窗、關掉記憶功能、開新對話。不然你看到的可能是「AI 對你個人的回答」。

4. 分開記四件事。  有沒有上網查、有沒有提到你、有沒有附你的網址、描述對不對。

5. 至少追兩週再談趨勢。  一天的起伏多半是雜訊。每個 AI 分開看，不要混在一起平均。

6. 不要用程式狂刷 Google。  違反 Google 的政策。需要大量量測，就走官方 API，或請專業團隊用合規的方式做。

如果你請別人幫你量，可以問對方五個問題：題目有幾題、幾種問法？每題問幾次？連續幾天？用 API 還是使用者介面？數字有沒有附信賴區間？  答不出來的報告，參考價值就要打折。

一句話收尾：AI 的回答是機率，不是名次。  量一次是運氣，量對了才是數據。

◆ 編按 · Think BIG 的做法

## 量得誠實、看得懂、可以驗證

（以下是 Think BIG 自己的立場，與上方中立報導區隔。）

我們的 AI 能見度報告，是照上面這套方法設計的，而且每份報告都把方法攤開：

一頁「分母與方法」：  幾題、幾種問法、每題重問幾次、量了幾天、哪些 AI、用什麼通道，全部寫清楚，你可以自己重問驗證。

觸發率單獨列：  AI 這次有沒有上網查。沒上網查的題目，靠的是模型記憶，改善方法和有上網查的題目不一樣。

描述對不對單獨列：  不只看 AI 有沒有提到你，也看它說的是不是事實，講錯的地方列出來追蹤修正。

每個 AI 各一套處方：  不同 AI 偏好的來源不一樣，所以建議也分開寫。

結論分級：  每個結論標明是【計數】、【對比】還是【推論】；區間重疊就寫持平，不美化。

我們不承諾名次或業績。我們承諾的是：量得誠實、看得懂、可以驗證。

### 常見問答 · FAQ

Q1：為什麼同一個問題問 AI，每次答案都不一樣？
AI 生成答案時本身帶有隨機性，引用的來源也會跟著變。瑞士聖加侖大學 2026 年的研究發現，同一題在同一天幾分鐘內重問，引用來源平均只重疊 32% 到 43%，和隔天重問差不多，表示變動主要來自模型本身，不是外在的演算法調整。
Q2：要知道 AI 會不會提到我的公司，要問幾次才夠？
依同一篇研究的推算，同一題每天至少問 7 次，才能把「被提到的比例」估得比較穩；要看引用來源，至少 8 次。時間上建議連續追蹤 10 天以上，用兩到四週的滾動區間來看趨勢。
Q3：可以寫程式自動查詢 Google 的 AI 模式來量測嗎？
不建議。Google 的垃圾內容政策禁止未經許可用程式自動查詢 Google 搜尋，包括為了查排名而抓取結果。合規的做法是使用各 AI 的官方 API，搭配人工抽查，並在報告中標明通道。
Q4：AI「提到」我和「引用」我有什麼不同？
提到是回答裡出現你的名字；引用是回答附上你的網頁連結當來源。兩者不一定同時發生，而且就算提到了，描述也可能不正確。建議分開記錄「有沒有提到」「有沒有引用網址」「描述對不對」。
Q5：有沒有官方工具可以看我的網站被 AI 引用的情況？
Bing Webmaster Tools 在 2026 年 2 月推出 AI Performance 報表（公開預覽），可以看到內容在 Copilot 與 Bing AI 摘要中被引用的次數與頁面。Google 這邊，AI 功能的流量會併在 Search Console 的「網頁」搜尋類型裡，無法單獨拆出。

參考來源
    Schulte、Bleeker、Kaufmann〈Don't Measure Once〉，聖加侖大學（2026-04；重疊度數字、7/8 次與 10/24 天門檻、ChatGPT 57.8% 無引用）：[arXiv 2604.07585](https://arxiv.org/abs/2604.07585)　·　Farquhar 等〈Detecting hallucinations in large language models using semantic entropy〉，Nature（2024）：[nature.com](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41586-024-07421-0)　·　〈GEO Critical Survey 2023–2026〉：[arXiv 2607.14035](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.14035)　·　Google 搜尋垃圾內容政策（機器產生的流量；2026-08-28）：[developers.google.com](https://developers.google.com/search/docs/essentials/spam-policies)　·　Bing Webmaster Blog〈AI Performance〉（2026-02-10）：[blogs.bing.com](https://blogs.bing.com/webmaster/February-2026/Introducing-AI-Performance-in-Bing-Webmaster-Tools-Public-Preview)　·　OpenAI 說明中心〈Searching the web with ChatGPT〉（記憶影響查詢改寫）：[help.openai.com](https://help.openai.com/en/articles/9237897-chatgpt-search)

# THINK BIG

Issue 004

GEO Measurement · AI Visibility

## Asked AI Once and Called It? — AI Answers Are Probabilities, Not Rankings: How to Measure GEO Properly

Think BIG Editorial  |  October 9, 2026

AI answers change every time. Re-ask the same question minutes apart and roughly two-thirds of the cited sources will be different. To know whether AI mentions you, ask repeatedly, track for weeks, and look at ranges — not single results.

## 1.  The problem: one screenshot proves nothing

“ChatGPT just recommended us!” “I asked three AIs and none of them mentioned us.” We hear both versions constantly. Behind each one is the same habit: ask once, treat it as the answer.  That works for traditional search, where the same keyword returns the same rankings minutes apart. AI doesn’t work that way.

A team at the University of St. Gallen published a paper in April 2026 titled “Don’t Measure Once,” studying this problem directly. From January to March 2026, they asked the same sets of questions to four AI search services (ChatGPT, Perplexity, Google AI Mode, Gemini) every day across four industries — 8 questions per industry — tracking continuously for 45–46 days and re-asking the same question up to 10 times within the same day. ([arXiv 2604.07585](https://arxiv.org/abs/2604.07585))

Key findings: day-to-day turnover is high.  Cited sources on consecutive days overlap only 34–42% on average. Same-day re-asks show the same instability:  re-asking minutes apart overlaps only 32–43% of cited sources — nearly the same as asking on different days. The researchers concluded the instability comes from how models generate text, not from external algorithm updates.

Brands are more stable than sources.  Brand mentions overlap 45–59% day-over-day, more than citation sources. Some questions are very stable, some aren’t at all.  Seeing just one or two questions reveals the personality of those questions, not your overall visibility.

AI doesn’t always search the web.  ChatGPT answered 57.8% of questions without any citations — because it only triggers web search for certain queries, and relies on model memory for the rest.

One line from the paper’s abstract fits as this article’s headline: AI search visibility should be described as a distribution , not a single data point .

## 2.  What the research says: how many times is enough?

The paper gives concrete thresholds.  To estimate “the rate at which a brand is mentioned” with enough stability (standard error below 0.10), you need at least 7 repetitions per question per day ; for citation sources, at least 8. For time, a single brand requires at least 10 consecutive days  to bring the standard error below 0.10, and 24 days to drop below 0.05. The authors recommend using a 2–4 week rolling window . They also advise: set a separate baseline for each AI, don’t average across AI tools; use brand mention rate as the primary signal and citation URL tracking as a diagnostic.

Repeated questioning also detects AI fabrications.  A 2024 Nature paper proposed: ask a model the same question multiple times; if the answers contradict each other, that’s a signal the model may be hallucinating. ([Farquhar et al., Nature 2024](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41586-024-07421-0)) One answer is a sample; repetition reveals the real picture.

Technique effectiveness can only be demonstrated with rigorous measurement.  A 2026 review of 45 GEO studies found that low source overlap and high run-to-run variability are pervasive in commercial audits; and no technique has been shown to improve discoverability stably, long-term, or across platforms. ([arXiv 2607.14035](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.14035)) If your measurement is noisy, you can’t tell whether a technique worked or you got a lucky sample.

But don’t break the rules to measure.  Google’s spam policies prohibit unauthorized automated queries to Google Search, including scraping for ranking data. The compliant path: use each AI’s official API, supplement with manual UI checks, and state which channel you used in every report.

Official data is now available.  Bing Webmaster Tools launched an AI Performance report in public preview in February 2026, showing how often your pages are cited in Copilot and Bing AI summaries, which pages are cited, and how that changes over time. ([Bing Webmaster Blog](https://blogs.bing.com/webmaster/February-2026/Introducing-AI-Performance-in-Bing-Webmaster-Tools-Public-Preview))

◆ First-hand notes

## 3. Three mistakes we made measuring our own AI visibility

Before launching our AI visibility service, we measured our own website first. We made three mistakes. All three are now written into our methodology.

Mistake 1: running one round and thinking we saw the truth.  Our first baseline was one question, one ask, one round. We barely showed up anywhere and felt discouraged. Then we checked Google Search Console and saw several of our guide pages ranked on the first page for their target queries. After reading the St. Gallen study, we confirmed: one round is statistically insufficient for any conclusion, positive or negative.

Mistake 2: a dirty test environment pollutes results.  On October 4, 2026, we ran a proxy test using an internal AI tool and found it had read notes stored on the test computer and incorporated them into answers. The results looked uncannily accurate — but that’s not what regular users see. OpenAI’s documentation notes that when memory is enabled, ChatGPT may use stored memories to rewrite search queries. Rule established: all measurements run in a clean environment — logged out, no conversation history, no memory, fresh session.

Mistake 3: treating “mentioned,” “cited,” and “described correctly” as the same thing.  AI can mention your name without linking to your page. It can link to your page while describing you incorrectly. We experienced this firsthand — an AI stated with complete confidence that our company had nothing to do with AI. Now every run records four things separately: did AI search the web, did it mention us, did it cite our URL, did it describe us accurately.

Our revised methodology in brief:

Item Our current practice
Questions Layered by intent: broad, contextual, conditional, brand comparison, factual; 3–5 phrasings per intent, including English versions

Lock questions Freeze the question set once built; add but never edit, so comparisons are valid over time

Repetitions Each question, each AI, multiple times per day with at least 10 minutes between runs

Duration Consecutive days; report on a 2–4 week rolling window

Separation Separate baseline for each AI; no cross-AI averages

Recording Did it search; was brand mentioned; position in answer; was URL cited; was description accurate

Reporting Every figure includes a 95% confidence interval; overlapping intervals between periods = “stable,” not “growth”

Channel State API vs. UI for each measurement; no automated scraping of Google pages

## 4.  Six principles for checking AI visibility yourself

1. Ask the same question several different ways.  Think like a customer: “Which [service] companies do you recommend in [city]?” “What’s good for a five-person company?” “How does A compare to B?”

2. Ask each question at least 5–7 times.  Record how many of those times you were mentioned. Look at the rate, not just “yes or no.”

3. Use a clean environment.  Log out or use a private window, disable memory, start a fresh session. Otherwise you’re seeing a personalized answer, not a representative one.

4. Track four things separately.  Did it search the web; did it mention you; did it cite your URL; did it describe you accurately.

5. Track for at least two weeks before talking about trends.  One-day fluctuations are mostly noise. Look at each AI separately — don’t average across platforms.

6. Don’t scrape Google.  It violates Google’s policies. For large-scale measurement, use official APIs or work with a team that does it compliantly.

If you’re evaluating a GEO vendor, ask five questions: How many questions, how many phrasings? How many repetitions per question? How many consecutive days? API or UI? Do the numbers include confidence intervals?  If they can’t answer, discount the report.

Bottom line: AI answers are probabilities, not rankings.  One ask is luck. Doing it properly gives you data.

◆ Editor’s note · How Think BIG approaches this

## Honest numbers. Readable reports. Verifiable methods.

(The following reflects Think BIG’s own position and is separate from the neutral reporting above.)

Our AI visibility reports follow this methodology and lay the method open in every report:

One “denominator and method” page:  how many questions, how many phrasings, how many repetitions per day, how many days, which AIs, which channel — all stated. You can re-run any query and verify.

Trigger rate listed separately:  did AI search the web for this question? Questions AI doesn’t search require different interventions than ones it does search.

Description accuracy listed separately:  not just whether AI mentioned you, but whether what it said was true. Inaccuracies are logged and tracked for correction.

Separate recommendations per AI:  different AIs favor different sources, so recommendations are split by platform.

Tiered conclusions:  each finding is labeled [count], [comparison], or [inference]; overlapping confidence intervals between periods = “stable,” not “growth.”

We don’t promise rankings or sales. We promise honest numbers, readable reports, and methods you can verify.

### FAQ

Q1: Why does the same AI question get different answers each time?
AI models introduce randomness when generating answers, and the sources they cite change along with the answer. A 2026 University of St. Gallen study found that re-asking the same question minutes apart overlaps only about 32–43% of cited sources on average — roughly the same as asking on consecutive days. The instability comes from how models generate text, not from external algorithm changes.
Q2: How many times do I need to ask AI the same question to get a reliable result?
The same study estimates you need at least 7 repetitions per question per day for brand mention rates, or 8 for citation rates, to bring the standard error below 0.10. For tracking trends, you need at least 10 consecutive days. The authors recommend using a 2–4 week rolling window.
Q3: Can I write a script to automatically query Google AI Mode for measurement?
No. Google’s spam policies prohibit automated queries to Google Search without permission, including scraping for ranking data. The compliant approach is to use each AI’s official API alongside manual spot-checks, and to document which channel you used in your report.
Q4: What’s the difference between AI “mentioning” me and “citing” me?
A mention means your name appears in the answer. A citation means the answer links to your page as a source. They don’t always happen together — and even when both occur, the description of your company may still be inaccurate. Track them separately.
Q5: Is there an official tool to see how often AI cites my website?
Bing Webmaster Tools launched an AI Performance report in public preview in February 2026, showing how often your pages are cited in Copilot and Bing AI summaries. On the Google side, AI-driven traffic is rolled into the “Web” search type in Search Console and can’t be broken out separately.
